Our first product / In development

Just a
better lamp.

A familiar switch.
A lamp that learns your evenings.

We're designing a table lamp that learns from ordinary use, so the light can be there when you need it. Put it down, plug it in and use the switch.

Watch the idea ↓

One on/off button.No app or account.No routine to program.

From the first use

You already know
how to use it.

Press the button for light. Press it again to switch off.

The lamp should work from the first evening, before it has learned anything. There is no pairing, clock setting or room calibration to complete.

Over time, repeated on/off choices would help it recognize when light is usually useful. The goal is fewer trips to the switch, with the same familiar control whenever you want it.

An example evening

Your routine is
the starting point.

Imagine you usually switch on between 5 and 6 pm, and off between 9 and 10 pm. Here is the behavior we're designing around that pattern.

  1. First eveningsYou use the switch.

    Ordinary use teaches the routine.

    Your repeated manual choices provide the examples. The lamp begins as a normal lamp, and assistance waits for a consistent pattern.

  2. Around 5 to 6 pmLight when it's useful.

    Timing and the room need to agree.

    In a learned evening window, the light could come on when you're nearby and the area is dark enough. The time alone should not switch it on in an empty or already bright room.

  3. Around 9 to 10 pmLight for late reading.

    A usual bedtime is not an instruction.

    The lamp should stay on while you're using the area. If you leave during a learned switch-off window, sustained absence could allow a gradual fade to off. Darkness alone should never trigger it.

  4. Whenever tonight changesYour choice comes first.

    The switch takes priority.

    A manual change should act immediately and prevent the lamp from promptly reversing it. Pressing during an automatic fade should restore the light. Repeated corrections should make the assistance back off.

Illustrative routine, not a demonstration or a fixed schedule. Learning time and automatic behavior still need to be tested in homes.

How it would know

A few useful clues,
close to the lamp.

The design combines your switch use with nearby light and presence.

A small computer inside the base would learn recurring choices and compare them with what's happening nearby. Light sensing helps judge whether more light is useful. Presence sensing helps avoid switching off while someone is still there.

After an automatic action, the lamp should check that its light responded. When the observations are unclear, it should preserve your manually selected state.

When other lights go out

A darker room is one clue, not permission to turn off. A single lamp cannot know whether every light in the house is off. The design only uses the area it can observe.

Designed to work on its own

The learning
stays in the lamp.

You should not need another device to use this one.

The design runs its core light control and learning locally, without Wi-Fi, an account, a companion app, a subscription or other connected lights.

It uses light and presence sensing, without a camera or microphone. Your manual choices teach preferences; the lamp's own automatic actions do not count as proof that it got them right.

A later change in routine should be learned through ordinary use. There is no schedule to edit or clock to set.

The thinking behind it ↗

Living with it

A few practical questions.

How many days would it take to learn?+

We haven't established a reliable number yet. The design needs repeated, consistent manual choices across different days, together with useful light and presence observations. An irregular routine should mean less automatic assistance, while the switch continues to work normally.

What if I sit still with a book?+

Keeping the light on for a still reader is a requirement. The proposed sensing includes still presence, but it must be tested across seats, postures and rooms. Uncertain presence should prevent automatic switch-off.

What if I move it or the power goes out?+

The design retains learned patterns during normal unplugging. A changed room can make those patterns less useful, so current observations still need to agree. If timing information is lost, timed assistance should pause until relearned. After power returns, the light is intended to stay off until you press the button.

Can I just use it as an ordinary lamp?+

Yes, ordinary on/off use is the starting requirement. There is no separate learning mode to select, and no setup required before you can use the switch. Your manual choice takes priority over automatic assistance.

Where the work stands

Designed.
Next, built and tested.

We have a proposed form, component choices and a plan for how learning and manual control should work together.

We have not yet built or tested a physical prototype. The next work is to establish comfortable light, reliable control and whether the assistance is useful in ordinary rooms.

Keep the light useful.
Test still reading, nearby lamps, changing daylight and unexpected interruptions.
Keep control familiar.
Check manual corrections, changing routines and behavior after unplugging.
Make a dependable object.
Measure light quality, heat and standby power, then test stability and upkeep.
